ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Constitution of Asian Economic Community 
*321. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Wiil th e Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government have initiated steps towards constitution 
of an Asian Economic Community on the lines of European Union (EU); 
(b) if so, the prec ise constitution and modus operandi of the 
contemplated Economic Community and India's role therein; and 
(c) the progress made in this regard, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) and (b) India has put forward the idea 
of a broader Asian Economic Community comprising India, ASEAN, Japan, 
China and Republic of Korea. 
(c) The concept of an Asian Economic Community has evoked 
considerable interest and positive re sponse from a number of countries 
as well as leading think tanks and academic organizations in the region. 
DR. AKHILESH DAS: Sir, our Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singhji, 
on the eve of his visit to Laos, while-addressing the ASEAN business 
summit, spoke of his vision of ASEAN economic community. May I know 
from the hon. Minister what precisely is the concept of the Prime Minister's 
vision in regard to the areas of cooperation in various fields of economy, 
whether it goes beyond the creation of free trade areas? If so, to what 
extent? 
SHRI E. AHAMMED: Mr. Chairman, Si r, the Prime Minister, in the 
third India ASEAN summit held in Vientiana Lao PDR on 30th November, 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2004] 
2004 proposed that in order to explore the idea further, and enthuse it 
with political direction, a workshop be held next year, with the 
participation of policy-makers, senior officials, industry and business 
representatives, to take the idea forward. I may be permitted to quote a 
portion of the statement of the hon. Prime Minister, which he had made 
in the 3rd India ASEAN business Summit, held in New Delhi on 9th 
October, 2004. 
'This community would constitute an arch of advantage across whid 
there would be large scale movement of people, capital, ideas and creativit 
Such a community would be roughly the size of the European Union I 
terms of income, and bigger than NAFTA in terms of trade." Therefore, 
Sir, we have been taking steps in line with what has been proposed by 
our hon. Prime Minister. 
DR. AKHILESH DAS: Sir, my sec ond supplementary is, the 21st 
century defined by human capital and knowledge, according to which, 
India holds the foremost position. How does the Government propose to 
ensure that India's dominant position in these areas is maintained so as 
to benefit India's economy, along with that of other members of the 
contemplated ASEAN economic community? 
SHRI E. AHAMMED: Sir, recently, we also have proposed this new 
concept in the second India ASEAN summit held in Bali in October, 2003. At 
that time also, the then Prime Minister had said that he was taking the opportunity 
of the complete presence of the other 13 countries to sow the seeds of a more 
ambitious idea. Thereafter, our Prime Mi nister also has made an elaborate 
statement on this matter, and I quote a por tion of his statement. "It is inevitable 
that we seek to take the existing India ASEAN relationship to a higher level, 
where we ambition an ASEAN economic community, which encompasses 
ASEAN, China, Japan, Korea and India. It is with this view in mind that the 
Government will be taking steps, as I have mentioned earlier. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the concept of the broader 
ASEAN economic community is indeed powerful and visionary one, 
because it will cover half the population of the world. Would the Minister 
kindly let us know what short of follow up action is planned for this? Is it 
just an idea that is being floated, or, will it be actively followed up in 
various fora? Secondly, is there any kind of broad timeframe, of five 
years or ten years, whthin which th is sort of an idea could actually 
materialise? 
2 

[23 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI E. AHAMMED: Sir, regarding the first question that the hon. 
Member has put, I would like to say that a workshop will be held, and it has 
been entrusted to one of the prominent think tanks of our country, i.e., the 
Research and Information Systems for non-aligned and developing countries. 
That is one of the think tanks here. They will bring the necessary framework 
for the workshop, and along with that, we are having negotiations with other 
countries in the region, how we will be able to have this community as early 
as possible. But every country has its own FTA, and also the RAC, with 
various countries. Taking into account their details, they will be responding 
to us. We hope that we will be able to go ahead without much delay, but a 
timeframe has not been fixed so far. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, the objective of an economic cooperation area 
is a very commendable one because it will  provide a lot of growth and trade 
opportunities to India. It has variously been called 'JACIK', standing for Japan, 
ASEAN, China, India and Korea. And also, it has been called the ASEAN 
plus four formula, ASEAN and these four countries, including India. 
Unfortunately, China is lukewarm to this proposal because it has earlier been 
pursing a formula known as ASEAN plus three, which includes all these 
countries except India. Sir, if that is the case, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister what steps his Ministry is taking to counter this attitude. 
SHRI E. AHAMMED: Sir, we are having negotiations with all countries, 
including China. It is premature for me  to say what each and every country 
has responded to, but I have the list of countries which have positively 
responded-lndonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and many other important 
countries. Sir, as I have mentioned earlier, in this workshop, India's 
approach is not exclusive. However, it is a starting point. The natural 
compostion in this regard would be India, ASEAN, Japan, China and the 
Republic of Korea. We have been going ahead on this line. We are going 
to take further steps on this line. 
SHRI FALIS. NARIMAN: Sir, the hon. Minister's conjoint answer to 
questions (a) and (b) prompts me to ask him this question. Question (b) 
was particularly concerning the precise constitution and modus operandi 
of the contemplated economic community; that is why, I am prompted 
only to ask the hon. Minister-this is a very enviable initiative-whether this 
is only a unilateral step or whether there is a hope for a consensus amongst 
the ASEAN countries or Japan, China and the Republic of Korea, because, 
actually, as everybody knows, the idea for a European Union was originated 
by Jean Monet who is now known as the Father of the European Union,

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2004] 
and this is a very laudable idea of the hon. Prime Minister, and of the 
Minister himself. But I would like to know whether this is merely a unilateral 
step or whether there has been some cooperation, apart from the think tanks of India, 
between the countries of Japan, China and the Republic of Korea. 
SHRI E. AHAMMED. Hon. Chairman, Sir, may I say that from 
the responses, which we have received from the countries, ASEAN, China, and 
also other regions, including Japan, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand, we feel 
that all of them are in agreement with this idea. However, as I mentioned 
earlier, when the think tanks and the research information centres of non-aligned 
and other developing countries start the process of this workshop, as it is 
scheduled, we will be in a better position to say how we will get 
the cooperation and how we will be able to have this ASEAN 
Economic Community. 
SHRI ANANO SHARMA: Sir, the initiative is indeed a 
commendable one. Everybody agrees with the hon. Prime Minister that this 
initiative, once it fructifies, will ensu re greater economic cooperation in the 
region which will be one of the largest economic unions. I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister, besides involving the think tanks, as he has stated—the think tank 
initiative is only the initial sounding—whether the Government of India will consider 
taking an official initiative in identifying a core group of countries which have 
positively responded to have a preparatory meet, as was done in the case of IOR 
(Indian Ocean Rim). I would also like to know from the hon. Minister whether the 
chambers of commerce and industry in India would be actively involved in the 
interaction with the chambers of commerce and industry in these countries which 
have been named and whether, simultaneously, we would try to have another meet 
so that this process gets accelerated. 
SHRI E. AHAMMED: Mr. Chairman, Sir, as regards the contacts at 
the official level, it is going on. The other part of the question of the hon. 
Member to have interaction with th e chambers of commerce and industry, 
etc., it is a very good suggestion for consideration. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Next question, Q. No. 322.

Funds for poverty eradication 
*322. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether inadequate funds are blocking developmental goals to 
reduce poverty to half by the year 2015; 
(b) whether the funds released by Government are not reaching to 
the poor; and 
(c) if so, the action proposed to step up efforts to remove economic 
hurdles, to build up proper administration for fulfilment of millennium goals 
to eradicate poverty? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
† Transliteration of Urdu speech.

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2004] 
Statement 
(a) The Millennium Development Goal aim at halving the proportion of people 
living below the poverty line by 2015 as compared to the level  prevailing in 1990. On 
current trends, it is expected that India will be able to achieve this target. Availability of 
funds is only one of the factors for reduction in poverty, and may not be a constraint to 
reduce poverty by half by 2015. 
(b) The Government is not aware of any study that shows that the 
funds released by the Government are not reaching the poor. The major welfare schemes 
targeted to the poor include Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana (SGRY), Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Indira Awaas Yojana 
(IAY), Swaran Jayanti Shahri Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), Targeted Public Distribution 
System (TPDS) and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY). However, the Government is 
aware that there is room for improvement in the delivery of some of these schemes. 
The Planning Commission will review the effectiveness of the delivery mechanism at 
the time of the mid-term review of the Tenth Plan. 
(c) The implementing Ministries have systems of monitoring through mechanisms 
such as periodic progress reports, inspection by Government officials, Area-
Officers' scheme, Performance Review Committees etc. In addition, regular impact 
assessment studies and evaluations of specific schemes are also undertaken. Further the 
release of funds is subject to receipt of Utilisation Certificates and Audit Reports. 
Based on programme evaluation and review, the schemes have been restructured and 
redesigned from time to time. Apart from capacity building of the individuals through 
human development strategies, involving access to education, basic health care facilities 
and opportunities of livelihood, the Tenth Plan strategy clearly aims at improving 
efficiency of public assets and the quality of expenditure of the public sector through zero 
based budgeting, monitoring and evaluation of plan programmes/  schemes, using e-
governance and IT for public government interfaceand thus increase transparency and 
make systems faster and user friendly.

Eligibility Criteria for Temporary Deputation to Consulate General 
of India, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia 
ADMINISTRATIVE PERSONNEL 
A. Eligibility Conditions: 
* Only Central and State Govern ment employees are eligible. 
Persons working in Public Sector Undertakings/Corporations, 
Autonomous Bodies. Subordinate offices, Colleges/Universities 
(except Central Universities)/Aided  Schools etc. are ineligible 
and need not apply. 
* For Assistant Haj Officer, the applicant should be Gazetted Officer 
serving in the grade of Section Officer of Central Government or 
equivalent in the pay scale of 6,500-200-10,500. Under Secretaries 
& above are not eligible for selection as AHOs and as such need 
not apply. 
* For Haj Assistant, the applicant should be holding a non-Gazetted 
post in the pay scale of Rs. 5,500-175-9000 and not below the 
grade of an Upper Division Clerk of Central Government or 
equivalent in pay scale of Rs. 4000-100-6000.

years of age as on 1st January. 
* The applicant should be medically fit and produce a Certificate to 
this effect from a Government Hospital. 
112 

[23 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA

* The applicant who have already performed Haj duty thrice or more 
are not eligible. 
* Applications of officers in the higher grade than prescribed shall 
not be entertained. 
B. Desirable Qualifications: 
* Due weightage will be given to applicants having knowledge of 
regional languages. 
* Weightage will be given to the applicants having experience in 
public relations and accounts. 
* Preference will be given to appli cants having knowledge of Data 
Entry and Computer Programming. 
MEDICAL AND PARAMEDICAL PERSONNEL 
A. Eligibility Conditions: 
* For Doctors: the applicant should be presently serving in a Central/ 
State Government Hospital or dispensary and must have a 
minimum of five years' experien ce as Medical Officer. Preference 
will be given to Doctors workin gas Medical Officer. Doctors holding 
senior posts or working as Professors/Readers, Medical 
Superintendents/Deputy Medical Superintendents etc. need not 
apply. 
* Only Allopathic Doctors (Gene ral Practioners)/Specialists 
Gynaecologists, ENT, Ophthalmologists, Pediatricians and 
Cardiologists need apply. Surgeons need not apply. 
* For Paramedics: the applicant should be in possession of Degree/ 
Diploma in Nursing/ECG/Lab. Technician. Minimum five years' 
service is essential. Auxiliary Nurses/Midwives need not apply. 
* Pharmacists should be in possession of B. Pharma Degree/ 
Diploma.

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2004]

January. However for Lady Doctors the age limit is 50 years.

Abolition of child labour 
2301. SHRI MAM. RAMASWAMY: W ill the Minister of LABOUR 
AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a number of States have failed in abolishing the menace 
of child labour for their respective States despite repeated directions from 
Government and the Supreme Court; 
(b) if so, the details of such States and the details of industries in 
which these child labour exists; 
(c) whether it is a fact that many children have lost their lives working 
in these factories/industries; 
136 

[23 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the details thereof, State-wise; and 
(e) the effective steps taken or proposed to be taken by the Central 
Government to end this menace at the earliest? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRASEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) In accordance with the provisions of the Child 
Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986, the National Policy on Child Labour 
was formulated by the Union Government in 1987. The policy envisages a sequential 
action-oriented approach for the abolition of child labour. The State Governments are 
implementing this policy as well as the verdict of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Writ 
Petition (Civil) No. 465/86 on 10.12.1996. However, child labour is a problem 
which is socio-economic in nature and is a result of poverty and illiteracy in the 
society. The fundamental problem regarding poverty and illiteracy need to be tackled 
effectively in order to abolish the menace of child labour from our country. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) The problem of child labour requires to be dealt through sustained 
efforts and the Government is committed to the goal of elimination of child labour 
in ali its forms. Considering the nature and magnitude of the problem, a gradual and 
sequential approach has been adopted to withdraw and rehabilitate child labour 
beginning with the children working in the hazardous occupations and processes. 
The action plan adopted by the Government to eliminate child abour comprises of 
legislative measures, general development programmes for benefiting children and a 
project based action plan in areas of high concentration of child labour. Under 
the NCLP Scheme, the children are withdrawn from work and put into special 
schools. They are provided basic education, vocational training, mid-day meal and 
health check up in order to prepare them to be mainstreamed into formal 
schooling system. During the Ninth Plan, the NCLP Scheme was implemented in 
100 districts of 13 child labour endemic states. The number of districts has been 
expanded to 250 districts in 20 States during the Tenth Plan.

safety and efficacy of new drugs is undertaken on the basis of results of 
various phases of clinical trials' data conducted by firms/organizations

features are given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
(b) The policy measures endorsed by National Road Safety Council 
are being implemented over a period of time. 
(c) and (d) These measures are reviewed by the National Road Safety 
Council periodically. Some of the important steps taken by the 
Government besides highway design to enhance road safety are as under: 
 
(1) Cranes and ambulances are pr ovided to various State 
Governments/NGOs under Nationa l Highway Accident Relief

(2) Grants-in-aid to voluntary organisations for administering road 
safety programmes. 
(3) Publicity campaign on road safety awareness through audio- 
visual-print media. 
(4) Encouraging use of simulators in driver's training. 
(5) Institution of National Award for voluntary organisations/individual 
for outstanding work in the field of road safety.

children with a view to create awareness. 
(7) Tightening of fitness norms for transport vehicles. 
(8) Widening and improvements of National Highways etc.

been steadily decreasing as under:-

(e) Road Safety Policy is constantly  reviewed by the Government to 
make it more effective keeping in view the changing environment. 
Statement 
The salient features of the National Road Safety Policy are:- 
* Classification of the cause of accident and preventive action in 
terms of vehicle, driver, and engineering aspects. 
* Safety features for vehicle de sign, Fitness certification and 
maintenance of vehicles. 
* Proper training and effective licensing for drivers. 
* Road design and geometric improvements. 
* Design of road junctions, accide nt black spot investigation 
and rectification. 
* Traffic guidance, road signs, speed limit posts, and other traffic 
control devices. 
* Road pavement markings, construction of footpaths/cycle 
tracks, truck parking complexes, and other way side 
amenities, etc. 
* Traffic education and campaign on traffic discipline including 
traffic education in school curriculum, etc. 
* Enforcement of maximum speed limits, and campaign on 
helmet, seat belt usage, drunken driving, etc. 
* Emergency medical service with emphasis on saving the lives
